newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks seen reporting glowing H1 results.
newsitem.headline: German banks seen reporting glowing H1 results.

text.p: Germany's top commercial banks are set to provide a glowing set of half-year results from next week, benefiting from the exceptional share market rally which has flooded their coffers with commission and trading income.
Analysts say that even if earnings growth slows during the second half of the year, the banks are well on course to post record profits for 1997.
"Everyone's buying shares," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank in Duesseldorf. "Earnings will hit records this year provided that financial markets don't collapse."

Bank shares have jumped in recent weeks in anticipation of good results but also amid renewed market speculation of mergers in the sector following news of a link-up between two insurers under the control of Munich Re.

And with share prices rising across virtually all sectors, the banks' industrial shareholdings have been transformed from burdens into a valuable source of future income as banks are expected gradually to divest the stakes, analysts said.

"The banks will have earned very much in the first half due mainly to the favourable market climate which will be reflected in commission and trading income," Nathalie Grasegger, analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank, wrote in a note to investors.

Market leader Deutsche Bank AG kicks off the reporting season with a news conference on Wednesday. Analysts on average expect it to report net income of 1.36 billion marks ($758 million), up 16.2 percent from the first half of 1996, under International Accounting Standards. Predictions range from 1.28 billion marks to 1.459 billion.
Operating profit after risk provisions is forecast at 2.74 billion marks on average, up 6.7 percent, with forecasts ranging from 2.6 to 2.95 billion.

Analysts said Deutsche's results, although buoyed by strong income gains, have been burdened a leap in administration costs caused in part by the mark's weakness against pound sterling and the dollar this year.

Deutsche is more exposed than its domestic rivals to currency movements because it employs roughly a third of its staff abroad following the rapid expansion of London-based investment banking arm Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
In addition, with performance-related pay prevalent in the investment banking community, many bankers will have received fat bonuses paid in increasingly expensive pounds sterling.

Deutsche's year-on-year earnings growth in the first half will also be squeezed because the bank last year dissolved about 600 million marks in pension provisions and no longer has the earnings benefit from that this year.

Germany's number-two bank, Dresdner Bank AG, presents its results at a news conference on July 29. Analysts forecast operating profit after risk provisions of 1.67 billion marks on average, up 17.5 percent. Forecasts range from 1.6 billion to 1.8 billion marks.
Commerzbank AG, the third-largest listed commercial bank, is due to release its results on Thursday. Analysts expect an operating profit of 1.44 billion marks on average, a rise of 8.4 percent.
The increase is expected to be relatively modest because Commerzbank's risk provisions were relatively light in the first half of 1996, followed by a sharp rise in the latter half.
That means that year-on-year, risk provisions for the first half of 1997 rose strongly, thereby squeezing earnings.
Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, which also publishes its results on Thursday, is forecast to publish operating profit of 815 million marks on average, up 22.6 percent.
Finally, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, the sector's number five, is expected to publish an operating profit of 686.5 million marks on average, up 23.5 percent.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
($ = 1.793 German Marks)
